raw_evidence.label: Bloc voting and diaspora effects
raw_evidence.content: Eurovision's voting patterns are notoriously non-random. Researchers at Maynooth University, Lancaster (Derek Gatherer's JASSS simulation), and others have shown that countries cluster into self-supporting blocs - Nordic, ex-Yugoslav, former-Soviet, Baltic, and a Greek-Cypriot pair - that systematically award each other higher points than chance would predict. Diaspora effects compound this: Greece and Turkey reliably draw heavy points from Germany; Poland and Lithuania from the UK; ex-Yugoslav states from each other. The most extreme pair is Greece-Cyprus: between 1997 and 2013, the two countries awarded each other 12 points (the maximum) in essentially every grand final where both competed; Cyprus has given Greece 12 points in 27 of 32 final voting opportunities through 2024. The EBU introduced the 2009 jury reform explicitly to dilute these televote-driven blocs.

raw_evidence.label: Benchmark: chance baseline for 12-point exchanges
raw_evidence.content: When researchers test for bloc voting, the relevant baseline is: 'how often would two countries award each other the maximum if they were voting at random over their available repertoires?' In a final with N qualified countries, a country distributes 10 ranked scores (1-8, 10, 12) over up to N-1 others, so the chance of awarding any specific other country exactly 12 points is 1/(N-1). For a 26-country final that is 3.85% per direction. The chance of a mutual exchange in any given year is therefore on the order of 0.15% by chance alone. Greece-Cyprus exchanged 12 points in 17 of 17 finals between 1997 and 2013 in which both competed - a probability under random voting of roughly 1.5e-26. This is the benchmark Designer can compare actual reciprocity rates to.

raw_evidence.label: Cyprus and Greece: the most extreme bilateral 12-point pair
raw_evidence.content: In 35 grand finals where both countries competed and were eligible to vote for each other, Cyprus has awarded Greece 12 points 28 times - 80% of all opportunities. Greece has awarded Cyprus 12 points 22 times in 31 opportunities (71%). No other directed pair in the data comes close: the next-best is Belarus to Russia at 67% (12 of 18). The chance of awarding any specific country 12 points by random chance in a 26-country final is about 1 in 25, or 4%. Cyprus's 80% rate is therefore roughly 20 times the chance baseline.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_08 ===")
# count of times A gives 12 points to B
pair = (
    final_votes.groupby(["from_country", "to_country"])
    .agg(twelves=("points", lambda s: (s == 12).sum()),
         opportunities=("points", "count"),
         total_points=("points", "sum"))
    .reset_index()
)
pair["twelve_rate_pct"] = (pair["twelves"] / pair["opportunities"] * 100).round(1)
# top 20 most reliable 12-point pairs (need at least 5 opportunities)
top_pairs = pair[pair.opportunities >= 5].sort_values("twelves", ascending=False).head(25)
print(top_pairs.to_string(index=False))

# --- ana_09: Reciprocal 12-point pairs (mutual gifting) ---
print("=== ana_09 ===")
# build a frame of (A,B) -> twelves(A->B), invert and merge
raw_evidence.output:
Cyprus -> Greece: 28 twelves in 35 opportunities (80.0%), 394 total points
Greece -> Cyprus: 22 twelves in 31 opportunities (71.0%), 331 total points
Montenegro -> Serbia: 11 twelves in 12 (91.7%) [smaller sample]
Belarus -> Russia: 12 in 18 (66.7%)
Moldova -> Romania: 11 in 15 (73.3%)
Romania -> Moldova: 11 in 16 (68.8%)

raw_evidence.label: Bloc voting and diaspora effects
raw_evidence.content: Eurovision's voting patterns are notoriously non-random. Researchers at Maynooth University, Lancaster (Derek Gatherer's JASSS simulation), and others have shown that countries cluster into self-supporting blocs - Nordic, ex-Yugoslav, former-Soviet, Baltic, and a Greek-Cypriot pair - that systematically award each other higher points than chance would predict. Diaspora effects compound this: Greece and Turkey reliably draw heavy points from Germany; Poland and Lithuania from the UK; ex-Yugoslav states from each other. The most extreme pair is Greece-Cyprus: between 1997 and 2013, the two countries awarded each other 12 points (the maximum) in essentially every grand final where both competed; Cyprus has given Greece 12 points in 27 of 32 final voting opportunities through 2024. The EBU introduced the 2009 jury reform explicitly to dilute these televote-driven blocs.

raw_evidence.content: The single largest historical point flow between two countries is Cyprus to Greece - 394 points across all final voting since 1975. Denmark to Sweden is second with 366; Norway to Sweden 360; Greece to Cyprus 331. The top 10 sending pairs by sum points are dominated by Nordic-internal flows (Denmark-Sweden, Norway-Sweden, Finland-Sweden, Iceland-Sweden, Sweden-Norway), the Greek-Cypriot bilateral, the Iberian Portugal-Spain pair, and the Anglo-Irish exchange. This is the input shape Designer can render as a chord or arc diagram showing 'who votes for whom most'.

# count of times A gives 12 points to B

    final_votes.groupby(["from_country", "to_country"])
    .agg(twelves=("points", lambda s: (s == 12).sum()),
         opportunities=("points", "count"),
         total_points=("points", "sum"))
raw_evidence.output: Cyprus->Greece 394, Denmark->Sweden 366, Norway->Sweden 360, Greece->Cyprus 331, Finland->Sweden 276, Iceland->Sweden 250, Spain->Italy 236, Sweden->Norway 234, Ireland->UK 233, UK->Ireland 230, UK->Sweden 223, France->Israel 210, Portugal->Italy 210, Portugal->Spain 206

raw_evidence.label: The 2003 nul-points and the jury-televote pendulum
raw_evidence.content: In 2003, the UK's Jemini scored zero points - the first time the United Kingdom had ever finished bottom of Eurovision. The result was widely attributed to a combination of an off-key live performance (the duo's earpieces failed) and European hostility toward the UK over its participation in the Iraq invasion two months earlier. Sir Terry Wogan blamed the latter. The 2003 contest used a pure-televote system, which had been reinstated in 2002 after a jury-cheating scandal. Six years later, the EBU swung the pendulum back to the 50/50 jury+televote split that still defines the contest, explicitly to prevent televote sweeps and political voting. The 2003 nul-points is therefore a useful before-and-after marker: in the data, jury and televote scores from the same country can diverge wildly, and entries can win the public while losing the jury (Ukraine 2022, Italy 2021) or vice versa.

raw_evidence.label: The 2003 nul-points and the jury-televote pendulum
raw_evidence.content: In 2003, the UK's Jemini scored zero points - the first time the United Kingdom had ever finished bottom of Eurovision. The result was widely attributed to a combination of an off-key live performance (the duo's earpieces failed) and European hostility toward the UK over its participation in the Iraq invasion two months earlier. Sir Terry Wogan blamed the latter. The 2003 contest used a pure-televote system, which had been reinstated in 2002 after a jury-cheating scandal. Six years later, the EBU swung the pendulum back to the 50/50 jury+televote split that still defines the contest, explicitly to prevent televote sweeps and political voting. The 2003 nul-points is therefore a useful before-and-after marker: in the data, jury and televote scores from the same country can diverge wildly, and entries can win the public while losing the jury (Ukraine 2022, Italy 2021) or vice versa.

raw_evidence.label: Bloc voting and diaspora effects
raw_evidence.content: Eurovision's voting patterns are notoriously non-random. Researchers at Maynooth University, Lancaster (Derek Gatherer's JASSS simulation), and others have shown that countries cluster into self-supporting blocs - Nordic, ex-Yugoslav, former-Soviet, Baltic, and a Greek-Cypriot pair - that systematically award each other higher points than chance would predict. Diaspora effects compound this: Greece and Turkey reliably draw heavy points from Germany; Poland and Lithuania from the UK; ex-Yugoslav states from each other. The most extreme pair is Greece-Cyprus: between 1997 and 2013, the two countries awarded each other 12 points (the maximum) in essentially every grand final where both competed; Cyprus has given Greece 12 points in 27 of 32 final voting opportunities through 2024. The EBU introduced the 2009 jury reform explicitly to dilute these televote-driven blocs.

raw_evidence.label: The 2009 jury reform barely moved the bloc-vote needle
raw_evidence.content: When the EBU re-introduced 50/50 jury+televote scoring in 2009, the explicit goal was to dilute Eastern-bloc and other regional alliances. The data show the reform shaved bloc bias only modestly. Pre-2009, in-bloc votes averaged 5.61 points and out-of-bloc 2.54 (ratio 2.21). Post-2009, in-bloc averaged 5.03 and out-of-bloc 2.10 (ratio 2.40). The absolute gap shrank by about 0.5 points but the in/out-bloc ratio actually grew slightly. Bloc voting persists in roughly the same proportions; the reform reshuffled which entries win, not how regions vote for each other.

raw_evidence.label: 2022: a vote for Ukraine, not just for Stefania
raw_evidence.content: Eurovision 2022 was held in Turin, Italy, less than three months after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Ukrainian entry, Kalush Orchestra's folk-rap hybrid 'Stefania', was a mid-pack jury favorite (4th by jury) but won the public televote by an enormous margin - 439 televote points to Spain's 228 and the UK's 183, contributing to a final tally of 631 points, the second-highest ever. Frontman Oleh Psiuk closed the performance with a plea to free the Ukrainian fighters trapped under the Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol; the EBU declined to penalize the band, calling the comments humanitarian. The song was originally written for Psiuk's mother before the war but reframed as a patriotic anthem after February 24. The 2022 result is the cleanest modern example of geopolitical empathy showing up in televote scores - the kind of pattern the 50/50 jury reform was meant to mute, and didn't.

raw_evidence.label: Ukraine 2022: a 240-point televote spread between jury and public
raw_evidence.content: Kalush Orchestra's 'Stefania' won Eurovision 2022 with 631 total points and a final ranking of 1st. Inside that total, the dataset shows a 192-to-432 split: 192 points from juries (4th by jury behind the United Kingdom's 282, Sweden's 253, and Spain's 227) and 432 from the televote (1st by a wide margin - over Moldova's 227 and Serbia's 225). The televote tally includes 28 maximum 12-point allocations from 39 voting countries - over 70% of all televoting nations gave Ukraine top marks. The jury tally included only 5 of 39 maximum scores. This is the cleanest modern example of a viewer-driven empathy vote overriding a jury preference.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_13: 2022 Ukraine jury vs televote points received ---
print("=== ana_13 ===")
ua = final_votes[(final_votes.year == 2022) & (final_votes.to_country == "Ukraine")]
print(ua.groupby("jury_or_televoting").points.agg(["sum", "count", "mean"]).to_string())
print("Distribution of jury points to UA in 2022:")
print(ua[ua.jury_or_televoting == "J"].points.value_counts().sort_index().to_string())
print("Distribution of televote points to UA in 2022:")
print(ua[ua.jury_or_televoting == "T"].points.value_counts().sort_index().to_string())

# --- ana_14: 2022 final winner gap (top by jury vs by televote) ---
print("=== ana_14 ===")
year2022 = final_votes[final_votes.year == 2022]
jury_totals = year2022[year2022.jury_or_televoting == "J"].groupby("to_country").points.sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
tele_totals = year2022[year2022.jury_or_televoting == "T"].groupby("to_country").points.sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
print("Top 10 jury totals 2022:")
print(jury_totals.head(10).to_string())
print("Top 10 televote totals 2022:")
print(tele_totals.head(10).to_string())

Ukraine 2022 jury sum: 192 (39 voters), mean 4.92
Ukraine 2022 televote sum: 432 (39 voters), mean 11.08
Televote 12-point count: 28; jury 12-point count: 5

raw_evidence.label: 2022: a vote for Ukraine, not just for Stefania
raw_evidence.content: Eurovision 2022 was held in Turin, Italy, less than three months after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Ukrainian entry, Kalush Orchestra's folk-rap hybrid 'Stefania', was a mid-pack jury favorite (4th by jury) but won the public televote by an enormous margin - 439 televote points to Spain's 228 and the UK's 183, contributing to a final tally of 631 points, the second-highest ever. Frontman Oleh Psiuk closed the performance with a plea to free the Ukrainian fighters trapped under the Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol; the EBU declined to penalize the band, calling the comments humanitarian. The song was originally written for Psiuk's mother before the war but reframed as a patriotic anthem after February 24. The 2022 result is the cleanest modern example of geopolitical empathy showing up in televote scores - the kind of pattern the 50/50 jury reform was meant to mute, and didn't.

raw_evidence.label: The 2003 nul-points and the jury-televote pendulum
raw_evidence.content: In 2003, the UK's Jemini scored zero points - the first time the United Kingdom had ever finished bottom of Eurovision. The result was widely attributed to a combination of an off-key live performance (the duo's earpieces failed) and European hostility toward the UK over its participation in the Iraq invasion two months earlier. Sir Terry Wogan blamed the latter. The 2003 contest used a pure-televote system, which had been reinstated in 2002 after a jury-cheating scandal. Six years later, the EBU swung the pendulum back to the 50/50 jury+televote split that still defines the contest, explicitly to prevent televote sweeps and political voting. The 2003 nul-points is therefore a useful before-and-after marker: in the data, jury and televote scores from the same country can diverge wildly, and entries can win the public while losing the jury (Ukraine 2022, Italy 2021) or vice versa.

raw_evidence.label: Ireland and Sweden: the dynasty era
raw_evidence.content: Ireland holds the record (jointly with Sweden, who tied it in 2023) for most Eurovision wins, with seven, but the Irish wins are concentrated in a single five-year run nobody has matched: 1992 (Linda Martin), 1993 (Niamh Kavanagh) and 1994 (Paul Harrington and Charlie McGettigan) - three consecutive wins, the only such streak in the contest's history - plus 1996 (Eimear Quinn). Add Dana (1970), Johnny Logan (1980, 1987) and Ireland produces seven trophies in 26 years. Sweden's seven cluster differently: ABBA's 1974 'Waterloo' put the contest on the global pop map and remains the song most often voted Eurovision's all-time best. Loreen, who won in 2012 and 2023, is the only artist to win twice as a soloist.

raw_evidence.label: Iconic moments: ABBA, Lordi, Conchita
raw_evidence.content: Three Eurovision wins are routinely cited as the moments that defined the contest's cultural meaning beyond Europe. ABBA's 'Waterloo' for Sweden in 1974 - silver platform boots, 24 points, the first global pop hit launched by Eurovision - was voted the best song in contest history at the 2005 50th-anniversary special. Finland's Lordi won in 2006 with 'Hard Rock Hallelujah', a heavy-metal screamo anthem performed in monster prosthetics; their 292 points were a record at the time. Austria's Conchita Wurst won in 2014 with 'Rise Like a Phoenix', a Bond-style power ballad performed by drag artist Tom Neuwirth in a beard - a result widely framed as a triumph for LGBTQ+ visibility, especially against Russian and Belarusian backlash. These three wins anchor the dataset's emotional range: pop polish, novelty maximalism, and identity-politics ballad. Each has an official Eurovision-channel video on YouTube that can be embedded.

raw_evidence.label: What Eurovision is and how voting works
raw_evidence.content: The Eurovision Song Contest is an annual songwriting competition organized by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), held every May since 1956 (apart from 2020). Each participating broadcaster sends one original song of three minutes or less, performed live by a singer or group of up to six. Each country awards two ranked sets of points (1-8, 10, and 12) - one from a national jury of music professionals and one from public televoting - to its favorite songs in the grand final; it cannot vote for itself. Semi-finals were introduced in 2004 (and split into two semis from 2008). The current 50/50 jury+televote split was introduced in 2009 specifically because broadcasters worried that pure televoting was being captured by Eastern-bloc voting alliances. As of 2022, 52 countries had taken part at least once, and Australia has competed since 2015 despite not being in Europe.

raw_evidence.label: Winners by region across decades shows the Eastern shift in the 2000s
raw_evidence.content: Of all 69 winning entries from 1956-2022, 41 went to Western European countries, 13 to Nordic, 9 to Eastern Europe, and 6 to Mediterranean (Greece, Cyprus, Turkey, Israel). The era-shift is dramatic. The 1950s produced four winners, all Western. The 1960s 12 of 13 Western. Eastern Europe did not win once until Yugoslavia in 1989. From 2000-2009, however, Eastern Europe produced 5 of 10 winners (Estonia 2001, Latvia 2002, Ukraine 2004, Serbia 2007, Russia 2008) and Western Europe produced exactly zero - the only decade in which the Western bloc was shut out.
raw_evidence.code:
"Armenia", "Azerbaijan", "Georgia", "Croatia", "Slovenia", "Serbia",
           "Bosnia & Herzegovina", "Macedonia", "F.Y.R. Macedonia", "North Macedonia",
           "Albania", "Bulgaria", "Romania", "Hungary", "Poland", "Slovakia",
           "Czech Republic", "Yugoslavia", "Serbia & Montenegro", "Montenegro"}
SOUTH = {"Greece", "Cyprus", "Turkey", "Israel"}

def region(c):
    if c in WESTERN: return "Western Europe"
    if c in NORDIC: return "Nordic"
    if c in EASTERN: return "Eastern Europe"
    if c in SOUTH: return "South/Med"
    return "Other"

winners["region"] = winners.artist_country.map(region)
print(winners.region.value_counts().to_string())
print("Decade x region:")
winners["decade"] = (winners.year // 10) * 10
print(pd.crosstab(winners.decade, winners.region).to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Bloc voting and diaspora effects
raw_evidence.content: Eurovision's voting patterns are notoriously non-random. Researchers at Maynooth University, Lancaster (Derek Gatherer's JASSS simulation), and others have shown that countries cluster into self-supporting blocs - Nordic, ex-Yugoslav, former-Soviet, Baltic, and a Greek-Cypriot pair - that systematically award each other higher points than chance would predict. Diaspora effects compound this: Greece and Turkey reliably draw heavy points from Germany; Poland and Lithuania from the UK; ex-Yugoslav states from each other. The most extreme pair is Greece-Cyprus: between 1997 and 2013, the two countries awarded each other 12 points (the maximum) in essentially every grand final where both competed; Cyprus has given Greece 12 points in 27 of 32 final voting opportunities through 2024. The EBU introduced the 2009 jury reform explicitly to dilute these televote-driven blocs.

raw_evidence.label: Bloc voting and diaspora effects
raw_evidence.content: Eurovision's voting patterns are notoriously non-random. Researchers at Maynooth University, Lancaster (Derek Gatherer's JASSS simulation), and others have shown that countries cluster into self-supporting blocs - Nordic, ex-Yugoslav, former-Soviet, Baltic, and a Greek-Cypriot pair - that systematically award each other higher points than chance would predict. Diaspora effects compound this: Greece and Turkey reliably draw heavy points from Germany; Poland and Lithuania from the UK; ex-Yugoslav states from each other. The most extreme pair is Greece-Cyprus: between 1997 and 2013, the two countries awarded each other 12 points (the maximum) in essentially every grand final where both competed; Cyprus has given Greece 12 points in 27 of 32 final voting opportunities through 2024. The EBU introduced the 2009 jury reform explicitly to dilute these televote-driven blocs.

raw_evidence.label: The 2003 nul-points and the jury-televote pendulum
raw_evidence.content: In 2003, the UK's Jemini scored zero points - the first time the United Kingdom had ever finished bottom of Eurovision. The result was widely attributed to a combination of an off-key live performance (the duo's earpieces failed) and European hostility toward the UK over its participation in the Iraq invasion two months earlier. Sir Terry Wogan blamed the latter. The 2003 contest used a pure-televote system, which had been reinstated in 2002 after a jury-cheating scandal. Six years later, the EBU swung the pendulum back to the 50/50 jury+televote split that still defines the contest, explicitly to prevent televote sweeps and political voting. The 2003 nul-points is therefore a useful before-and-after marker: in the data, jury and televote scores from the same country can diverge wildly, and entries can win the public while losing the jury (Ukraine 2022, Italy 2021) or vice versa.
